study.title: Tendon loading: pain-guided progression dominates but isn't shown better than alternatives
study.evidence_note: Systematic review of 30 RCTs (Achilles, patellar, gluteal). No trial isolates the progression rule; narrative synthesis only.
study.confidence_note: PMC full text via extraction; appendices not read. Table 1 lists 31 trials vs 30 in text; poor-quality count 6 vs 4.
study.impact_line: Pain-monitored progression is convention, not proven superior. Keep it, but don't oversell it. Barely covers Achilles isometrics.
key_findings: 20 of 30 RCTs progressed load by tolerated pain, mostly Alfredson-style eccentrics
No trial compared the same programme with different progression rules
Achilles isometrics: one trial only; adding isometrics to eccentrics gave no extra benefit
Staged HSR vs pain-guided eccentrics (Beyer): larger change, not significant
Trial quality fair: PEDro mean 6.0, range 3 to 8
summary: Systematic review of 30 RCTs across Achilles, patellar and gluteal tendinopathy, most of them Achilles
Classifies progression rules: pain primary (evoke or avoid pain) or pain secondary (stages, fatigue, perception, fixed increase)
Pain-based rules seem inherited from early eccentric protocols rather than tested
Authors suggest individualised %RM loading may matter more than staging itself
Calls for head-to-head trials of progression criteria
study.bottom_line: No progression rule is proven better for Achilles tendinopathy. Pain-monitored loading is reasonable convention. This review offers nothing on isometrics for early-stage mid-portion Achilles pain; look to direct trials for that.

design: Systematic review of RCTs, narrative synthesis
setting: PubMed, Embase, Scopus, PEDro to 24 Sep 2020
participants: Adults 16+ with mid-portion Achilles, patellar or gluteal tendinopathy
intervention: Progressive exercise alone with a described load progression rule
Mostly eccentric; some HSR, concentric, isometric, isotonic
comparator: Another exercise programme, other treatments, or wait-and-see

results.result: Evoke pain 20, stages 8, perception 4, avoid pain 3
results.detail: Fatigue-based 1 (Horstmann), fixed 2.5% weekly increase 2 (Rio, van Ark). Some trials counted under two rules.

results.meaning: No extra benefit; CI and MCID check unavailable
results.detail: Table 2. Both arms progressed on avoid-pain and subjective perception rules. PEDro 5. Not an isometric-for-pain-relief protocol.

results.meaning: Can't judge vs VISA-A MCID (~10 points, inferred)
results.detail: Table 2. Exercise type and rule both differ, so the rule's effect can't be isolated. Large d yet non-significant suggests d may not be a between-group effect.

results.meaning: Not significant; can't claim it's no worse
results.detail: Table 2. Both arms pain-guided. Short follow-up only.

results.meaning: Loading beats no loading; rule untested
results.detail: Table 2: Rompe 49% vs 14% VISA-A change; Horstmann 67% vs 28%. No CIs. Extractor flagged Rompe as insertional; the 3-arm Rompe trial was likely mid-portion.

results.result: Rio favoured isometric for decline-squat pain; van Ark no difference
results.effect: Rio d 2.75, p<0.05; no CI reported
results.meaning: Patellar only; conflicting; transfer to Achilles inferred
results.detail: Table 2. Both progressed by fixed 2.5% weekly load. In-season athletes. Clifford (gluteal) isometric vs isotonic VISA-G d 0.005, no difference.
Table 4: therapist blinding 0%, participant 3.2%, assessor 38.7%, ITT 41.9%. Text says 6 poor; Table 4 shows 4.

full_text.why: Read in full from the free full text (PMC7678382 and BMJ Open). Fetches were model-summarised; supplementary appendices 2–3 not read.

how_to_apply: Keep pain-monitored loading for Achilles; this review shows no better rule.
Tell patients pain-guided progression is convention, not proven best.
Anchor load to a capacity marker too, such as reps or RM.
Don't add isometrics to eccentrics expecting extra VISA-A gains.
For early-stage isometrics, use direct Achilles trials, not this review.
applies_to: Adults with mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy on a loading programme
Patellar and gluteal tendinopathy loading, same caveats
Choosing and explaining a progression rule
not_for: Deciding if isometrics relieve early-stage Achilles pain

grade.reason: Trials mostly unblinded; PEDro mean 6.0; ITT in under half.
Mixed significant and null results across rules and comparators.
No trial varies only the progression rule; exercise type is confounded with the rule.
No pooled estimate or CIs; small trials; most comparisons non-significant.
Not formally assessed; many small trials and authors flag possible selection and reporting bias.

clinical_significance: Effects given as % change and Cohen's d, not VISA-A points, so MCID can't be checked
VISA-A MCID about 10 points (inferred; McCormack 2015 found 6.5 in insertional cases)
A meaningful difference between progression rules can't be ruled in or out
comparator_fairness: Comparators vary: other exercise, passive treatments, wait-and-see
Wait-and-see arms flatter loading but say nothing about the rule
alternative_explanations: Exercise type, volume and supervision differ alongside the rule
Natural history and regression to the mean in uncontrolled arms
Co-interventions: analgesics or NSAIDs allowed in some trials, no washout
spin: Little: conclusions say pain-based rules lack strong support
fit_with_evidence: Consistent with Malliaras 2013 review: no loading programme clearly superior for Achilles
Doesn't test isometric analgesia; later Achilles trials are needed for that
Fits Atlas Achilles playbook: progressive loading, pain-monitored
external_validity: ✓ Progressive loading as used in private sports physio
✗ Isometric data are mostly patellar, in-season athletes
✗ Participant ages and sport levels not summarised
would_change_my_mind: An RCT of one Achilles programme progressed by pain vs by capacity
An Achilles trial showing isometrics outperform isotonic loading early
weaknesses: Text and tables disagree on counts
Rule effect confounded by exercise type
appraisal.funding_conflicts: Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities FPU grant; University of Málaga paid open access. Authors declared no competing interests.

disagreements.why: Many small trials; authors flag selection and reporting bias.
disagreements.resolved: Agreed: serious. Certainty stays very low.

disagreements.why: No CI or margin, so non-inferiority can't be claimed.

disagreements.item: Style: provenance in transfer and methods

verification.external_searched: PEDro indexes it as a systematic review but no AMSTAR-type rating found. Web search for umbrella reviews rating it with AMSTAR 2: none found.

study.patient_explanation: There's no proven best way to step up tendon exercises. Using pain as a guide is common and reasonable: some discomfort is okay if it settles. We'll also track what you can do, like reps and load, to guide progress.
open_questions: Does pain-guided progression beat capacity-guided progression for Achilles?
Do isometrics help early-stage mid-portion Achilles pain more than isotonic loading?
What pain threshold during loading is safe and effective?

sources.citation: Escriche-Escuder A, Casaña J, Cuesta-Vargas AI. Load progression criteria in exercise programmes in lower limb tendinopathy: a systematic review. BMJ Open 2020;10(11):e041433.
